cards.explanation: The answer is the sons of Joseph. Chronicles says it flat out: Reuben's "…birthright was given to the sons of Joseph son of Israel…" (1 Chronicles 5:1). Reuben was first in line and still got passed over. Friends, that's like being first to the cookie table and finding the plate already empty. And he is not reckoned according to birthright.

The answer is ruler. "…a ruler came from him…" says Chronicles about Judah (1 Chronicles 5:2). Judah prevailed over his brothers. And still the birthright belonged to Joseph. That's two different blessings going to two different brothers.

The answer is livestock, friends! Chronicles says "…their livestock had increased in the land of Gilead." and that's why the Reubenites spread so far east (1 Chronicles 5:9). It's like when your garage fills up and your stuff starts creeping into the driveway. More animals meant they needed more room.

The answer is False. The text says the Hagrites "…were defeated at their hands…" (1 Chronicles 5:10). The Reubenites won that war. Then they moved into the Hagrites' dwellings throughout the region east of Gilead. That's a good day for them, friends.

The answer is that they cry out to God. "…because they cried out to God in battle, they were helped against their enemies…" (1 Chronicles 5:20). Right in the middle of the fight, they cried out to God. I'd say that's the best move you can make with 44,760 warriors standing right there.

The answer is that they put their trust in Him, friends. Chronicles says it plainly: "Because they put their trust in God, He answered their prayers." (1 Chronicles 5:20). The reason is right there in the verse. They cried out, and they trusted Him.

The answer is God, friends. "…many others fell slain, because the battle belonged to God." (1 Chronicles 5:22). The text puts the battle in God's hands, not theirs. That fits with verse 20, where they cried out to Him, put their trust in Him, and He answered their prayers.

The answer is unfaithfulness to God. The heads of Manasseh's families were "…mighty men of valor, famous men…" and then comes the turn: "But they were unfaithful to the God of their fathers…" (1 Chronicles 5:24-25). All that fame, and the story moves to unfaithfulness. I think this is a heavy part, friends, and it's worth a quiet pause.

The answer is True. The verse says they turned to "…the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them." (1 Chronicles 5:25). So those were peoples God had already destroyed before them. It's a serious detail, friends, and the text states it plainly.

The answer is the God of Israel. "So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria…" to take them into exile (1 Chronicles 5:26). Pul is also called Tiglath-pileser. That verse comes right after the unfaithfulness in verse 25. It's a sober ending to a passage that started with a birthright.
